why_it_matters: Any principal with s3:PutObjectAcl can mark an object public-read, making it readable by anonymous HTTPS GetObject requests.
Public ACLs bypass the bucket policy review that teams usually rely on, so exposure can happen through a single API call.
block_public_acls makes S3 reject the PutObjectAcl and PutBucketAcl requests that would grant public access.
post_en:
One false flag on an S3 public access block is enough for a single PutObjectAcl call to expose an object to the whole internet.

Checkov rule CKV_AWS_53 checks that aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block sets block_public_acls to true, so S3 rejects any request that tries to attach a public ACL to the bucket or its objects.

Why it matters: anyone with s3:PutObjectAcl or s3:PutBucketAcl, including a leaked CI credential or a well-meaning teammate, can grant public-read. Anonymous clients can then fetch the object with a plain HTTPS GetObject, no AWS credentials needed. The public access block is a bucket-level guardrail that overrides those ACLs even when someone gets them wrong later.

The fix: set block_public_acls = true (and its three siblings) on aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, and enforce BucketOwnerEnforced ownership so ACLs stop mattering at all.

Every snippet in this series is checked by Terraform and Checkov before it is posted: the misconfigured version must fail the rule and the fixed version must pass it.
